screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you'll build a practical understanding of containers with Docker and why containers matter for a Linux professional. We'll start by defining containerization and contrast it with virtual machines so you can see why containers are lighter and faster. Then we'll walk through installing the Docker Engine on a Linux host, verifying the installation, and running a simple container to confirm everything works. After that we explore images and containers — how to pull images from a registry and run them with common options like detached mode and port mapping. Finally you will learn how to author a simple Dockerfile, build a custom image, and run your own containerized web page. Think about a service you manage now — could it be packaged and moved between systems more reliably if it ran in a container?

screens.title: What is Containerization?
screens.narratorSegment: Containerization packages an application together with its runtime, libraries, and configuration so that the complete runtime environment moves as a single unit. For a Linux administrator that means fewer environment mismatches: a container carries the app and dependencies but uses the host kernel rather than a full guest operating system. In practice this makes containers much lighter and faster: starting a container takes seconds, while booting a full VM may take minutes. A concrete example is running a web server. With a VM you maintain a full OS image plus Nginx; with a container you package just Nginx and its minimal libraries and start it instantly. A common misconception is to treat containers as tiny virtual machines; this can lead to unnecessary duplication and heavier images. Instead, think of containers as isolated processes with limited scope and predictable file systems. When you design services, prefer each container to run a single concern and use configuration or orchestration for composition. Takeaway: containers improve portability and startup speed by sharing the host kernel, but they are not replacements for a full OS when you need separate kernels or deep hardware abstraction. How would you separate concerns in an application you support today so each part can run in its own container?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › What is Containerization?
Core Concept
What is Containerization?
Packaging an application with its dependencies while sharing the host kernel for efficiency and portability.

Definition: Containerization bundles app code, libraries, and configuration into a single, isolated runtime unit that uses the host kernel.

Why it matters: Containers start quickly, use fewer resources, and reduce the "works on my machine" problem between dev and production.

Concrete example: Package an Nginx server and its minimal dependencies as a container image and run it on your laptop or cloud VM with consistent behavior.

Misconception: Containers are not lightweight virtual machines; they do not include a full guest kernel and should not be treated like separate OS instances.

Analogy
A container is like a sealed shipping crate for a single service, not a whole warehouse.
Key Takeaway
Use containers to package apps for portability, but design them for single responsibilities.
Comparison snapshot
Container
Shares host kernel, fast start, smaller footprint.
Virtual Machine
Full guest OS, heavier, useful when separate kernels are required.
When to choose which
Use containers for services; use VMs when you need full OS separation or kernel-level features.

screens.title: Containers vs Virtual Machines
screens.narratorSegment: Let's contrast containers and virtual machines with concrete trade-offs a Linux engineer needs to know. Containers package applications and dependencies but share the host kernel. That means low overhead, faster startup, and greater density—more containers per host. Virtual machines emulate hardware and include a full guest OS, which increases resource consumption but provides a separate kernel and stronger isolation at the cost of slower provisioning. A practical scenario: running many identical microservices benefits from containers because each instance consumes fewer resources and starts quickly. Conversely, if you must run an alternative kernel version or isolate kernel modules, a VM is the safer choice. A common misconception is that containers automatically provide stronger security isolation than VMs. In reality, the kernel is shared, so policy, namespaces, and cgroups matter; containers should be combined with security controls when isolation is required. Example: on a test host you might run ten container instances of a web app; attempting the same with full VMs likely exhausts memory or C P U far sooner. Takeaway: pick containers for efficiency and portability, pick VMs when you need full OS separation or complete kernel isolation. Ask yourself: which constraints matter more—density and speed, or kernel-level separation?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Containers vs Virtual Machines
Quick comparison
Footprint
Containers: small. VMs: large.
Density
Startup
Containers: seconds. VMs: minutes.
Speed
Isolation
Containers: process-level. VMs: full OS-level.
Security trade-off
Scenario walkthrough
Imagine you need to run 12 identical stateless web service instances for load testing. Containers let you start many instances quickly with minimal RAM overhead. If instead you must run services requiring kernel modules not present on the host, you would choose VMs to isolate kernels.
Common misconception
Assuming containers always provide VM-level isolation can lead to insecure deployments. Use namespaces, cgroups, and additional kernel hardening when isolation is required.
Key Takeaway
Choose containers for efficiency and portability; choose VMs for kernel-level separation.

screens.title: Install Docker Engine on Linux
screens.narratorSegment: Installing Docker Engine on a Debian or Ubuntu system includes a few precise steps: prepare packages for secure transport, add Docker's GPG key so the repository is trusted, add Docker's stable repository, and then install docker-ce along with the CLI and container runtime. The commands shown in the lesson content are the recommended sequence. Practically, you will update apt, install supporting packages for HTTPS transport, register Docker's repository key, and then install docker-ce, docker-ce-cli and containerd. io. A crucial operational step is adding your user to the docker group so you can run docker commands without sudo; forgetting this step commonly results in permission denied messages. Takeaway: follow the install sequence exactly and verify with the hello-world run to ensure the engine operates correctly. Install Docker Engine on Linux means add repository, install docker-ce and dependencies, and add your user to the docker group to avoid permission errors.. In practical terms, repository, package, and group setup for debian/ubuntu. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Install Docker Engine
Process Flow
Install Docker Engine
Follow these steps to add the repository and install Docker on Debian/Ubuntu.
Step 1 — Prepare packages for HTTPS transport and certificate support.
Step 2 — Add Docker's official GPG key and repository to apt sources so packages are trusted.
Step 3 — Update apt and install docker-ce, docker-ce-cli, and containerd.io.
Step 4 — Add your user to the docker group and apply changes so you can run docker without sudo.
Common mistake
Forgetting to add your user to the docker group causes permission denied errors when running docker commands without sudo.
Terminal — installation commands
sudo apt update
sudo apt install apt-transport-https ca-certificates curl software-properties-common
curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/docker-archive-keyring.gpg
echo "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/docker-archive-keyring.gpg] https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu $(lsb_release -cs) stable" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list > /dev/null
sudo apt update
sudo apt install docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
newgrp docker
Run the last line to apply group changes immediately. After installation, verify with the hello-world run to confirm daemon operation.

screens.title: Verify Docker: hello-world and permissions
screens.narratorSegment: After installing Docker you must verify that the daemon is active and that you can run containers. A standard verification is to run the lightweight hello-world image. This image performs a simple runtime check and prints a success message when Docker can fetch and run an image. If the daemon is not running, the hello-world run will fail. Another common issue appears as a permission denied error when the current user is not in the docker group; you can fix this by adding the user to that group and applying the change immediately with a new group session. Concrete example: after installation run the hello-world image and then list running containers. If the hello-world image completes successfully it prints a confirmation message and exits; it may not leave a running container. Misconception: assuming a successful install means you can run long-lived services immediately without checking group membership and daemon status can lead to confusing failures during later steps. Key takeaway: always verify the daemon with hello-world and set correct permissions before moving to real services. Verify Docker: hello-world and permissions means run hello-world to check the daemon and add your user to the docker group to avoid permission denied errors.. In practical terms, confirming the daemon, running the test image, and avoiding permission errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Verify Docker
Run this check
The hello-world image verifies the engine can pull and run containers. It is lightweight and exits after printing a success message.
docker run hello-world
Expected result: a confirmation message. Troubleshooting: if you see permission denied, add your user to the docker group and reload your group session. If the daemon is inactive, start or enable the Docker service.
Pro tip
Use the hello-world check early to confirm the runtime before attempting to run networked services like Nginx.
Permission fix
Add your user to the docker group and apply group changes immediately so that docker commands work without sudo.
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
newgrp docker
After this, re-run the hello-world check. If you still see issues, inspect the docker daemon logs for startup errors before proceeding.

screens.title: Docker Images and Containers
screens.narratorSegment: Docker uses two fundamental artifacts: images and containers. An image is a build-time, read-only package that contains everything needed to run an application: code, libraries, system tools, and default settings. Images are built from a Dockerfile and composed of layers where each instruction typically creates a new layer that can be cached. A container is a runnable instance of an image — a process (or set of processes) with its own filesystem and namespaces. For example, you can pull the Ubuntu image from a registry and then instantiate a container from it to run commands inside that environment. This separation matters because you can build many identical containers from a single image; images are the portable artifact you store in registries such as Docker Hub. A common mistake is editing a running container's filesystem and assuming the change is preserved to a new image; instead, you should update the Dockerfile and rebuild so the change is reproducible. Takeaway: treat images as immutable build artifacts and containers as ephemeral runtime instances that you can stop and remove. How would you capture a change in configuration so it survives image rebuilds?

keyIdea.text: Images are build-time artifacts composed of layers; containers are the ephemeral, runnable instances created from images.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Images & Containers
Image
A lightweight, standalone package of software including code and dependencies. Images are built from Dockerfiles and stored in registries.
Layers
Each Dockerfile instruction creates a layer. Good Dockerfile ordering and small layers improve cache effectiveness and reduce rebuild time.
Example
Pull ubuntu:latest as an image, then create a container to run commands inside that environment.
Container
A runnable instance of an image. Containers have isolated filesystems and namespaces but share the host kernel.
Ephemeral
Containers are typically transient; stop and remove them when finished. Persist important state to volumes or rebuild images to include changes.
Common mistake
Modifying a running container and assuming the change becomes an image. Instead, update the Dockerfile and rebuild to capture the change reproducibly.

screens.title: Pulling and Running Images
screens.narratorSegment: Pulling an image retrieves it from a registry and stores it locally. Use the pull command to download an image before running it, although many run commands will pull an image automatically if it's missing. When you run an image as a container, common options include detached mode and port mapping so services are accessible from the host. For example, running an Nginx container mapping container port eighty to host port eight thousand eighty makes the web server reachable from a browser. Another important option is naming containers so you can refer to them easily when stopping or removing them. A frequent operator misstep is forgetting the port mapping and then wondering why the service is unreachable; always confirm the -p or port mapping semantics. Concrete example: pull the ubuntu image and run a shell, or pull the nginx image and run it detached while mapping ports. Takeaway: use pull to control when you fetch artifacts, and use docker run flags to configure networking and lifecycle behavior for the container instance. Pulling and Running Images means use docker pull to fetch images and docker run with flags like detached mode and port mapping to make services reachable.. In practical terms, fetch images from docker hub and run services with options. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Pull & Run
Commands
Pull an image explicitly or let docker run fetch it automatically when missing.
docker pull ubuntu:latest
# Run an nginx container detached and map host port 8080 to container port 80
docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name my-nginx nginx
After running, open http://localhost:8080 on your host or the VM's IP and port to see the Nginx welcome page.
Options to remember
  • Detached mode runs the container in the background so your terminal is free.
  • Port mapping binds container ports to host ports to expose services.
  • Name the container to refer to it easily with stop and rm.
Common mistake
Omitting port mapping means the container is running but inaccessible from the host; always confirm mapping when exposing services.

screens.title: Managing Containers with the Docker CLI
screens.narratorSegment: Managing containers is a routine daily task for Linux administrators working with Docker. The docker ps command lists running containers; adding the -a flag shows all containers including those stopped. To stop a running container cleanly, use docker stop followed by the container name or id, which allows the process to exit gracefully. After a container is stopped, remove it with docker rm to free resources. If you need to remove an image, use docker rmi with the image id. A common operational error is attempting to remove a running container without stopping it first; Docker will prevent that and prompt you to stop the container. Also be mindful that stopped containers and unused images consume disk space over time; schedule regular cleanup to reclaim space. Concrete example: run a container named my-nginx, confirm it with docker ps, then stop and remove it with stop and rm. Takeaway: learn the sequence: list, stop, then remove — and automate cleanup for environments with frequent image churn. Managing Containers with the Docker CLI means list running and stopped containers; stop before removing; remove unused images to reclaim disk space.. In practical terms, list, inspect, stop and remove containers safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Manage Containers
Common commands
# List running containers
docker ps
# List all containers, including stopped
docker ps -a
# Stop a running container
docker stop my-nginx
# Remove a stopped container
docker rm my-nginx
# Remove an image
docker rmi <image-id>
Remember: stop before remove. Use names to simplify the workflow when scripting or performing routine operations.
Cleanup guidance
  • Remove stopped containers regularly to free space.
  • Remove unused images that are no longer referenced by containers.
  • Consider automated pruning in development environments, but be cautious in production.
Common mistake
Neglecting to remove stopped containers and old images can gradually consume disk space and create confusing listings.

screens.title: Dockerfile Basics
screens.narratorSegment: A Dockerfile is the recipe Docker uses to build an image. Each instruction creates a layer that contributes to the final image: FROM selects the base image, RUN executes commands during build, COPY brings files from the build context into the image, EXPOSE documents ports the container listens on, and CMD declares the default command that runs when a container starts. Understanding these instructions helps you build small images and leverage build cache effectively. For example, pinning a base image like an explicit version reduces unexpected behavior but may require periodic updates. A concrete illustration is a small Python app: use FROM python with a slim tag, set WORKDIR, COPY requirements, RUN pip install, COPY the application code, and set CMD to run the app. A common misconception is to put frequent-changing files before dependency installation in the Dockerfile; this busts the cache and slows builds. Takeaway: order your Dockerfile to install stable dependencies first, then copy volatile source files, so iterative builds are faster and more reliable. When you write your Dockerfile, ask: which parts change often and should be placed after the cached steps?

keyIdea.text: Dockerfile instructions form layered builds; order instructions to maximize cache reuse and minimize rebuild time.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Dockerfile Basics
Key instructions
FROM sets the base image for the build.
RUN runs commands at build time to install packages or make changes.
COPY copies files from the build context into the image.
EXPOSE documents the ports used by the container at runtime.
CMD provides the default command to run when a container starts.
Best practice
Order Dockerfile instructions so stable steps run first and volatile source files are copied last to take advantage of build cache.
Example Dockerfile
# Dockerfile for a simple Python Hello World app
FROM python:3.9-slim-buster
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY hello.py .
CMD ["python", "hello.py"]
Build with docker build -t my-python-app . and then run the container. Adjust the base image tag to match your security and compatibility needs.

screens.title: Build and Run a Custom Image
screens.narratorSegment: Building a custom image turns your project files into a reusable artifact you can run anywhere Docker is available. The hands-on example in the chapter uses a lightweight Nginx base image. You place your index. html in a build context directory, write a Dockerfile that uses FROM nginx:alpine, COPY the H T M L into the Nginx web root, EXPOSE port 80 for documentation, and rely on the base image's default command to run Nginx. When you run docker build with the tag flag it creates an image with the given name in your local registry. A concrete sequence: create the directory, add index. html and a Dockerfile, run docker build -t hello-cohortia-web dot, then run the built image mapping host port eighty to container port eighty. A common misconception is that COPY alone makes content live on running containers; it only sets up the image. If the content changes, update the source and rebuild the image. Takeaway: build reproducible images by keeping application assets and Dockerfile together in the build context and rebuild whenever source files change. Build and Run a Custom Image means keep source files and dockerfile in the build context, build with docker build -t name ., and run with docker run and port mapping to expose services.. In practical terms, create a static web page image using nginx:alpine and dockerfile. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Build & Run
Hands-on steps
Create a directory with index.html and a Dockerfile, then build and run the image to serve your static page.
mkdir ~/my_web_app && cd ~/my_web_app
# index.html in the directory
# Dockerfile example shown on the right
docker build -t hello-cohortia-web .
docker run -d -p 80:80 --name cohortia-web hello-cohortia-web
Open http://localhost or the VM's IP to confirm your custom "Hello Cohortia!" page appears. Clean up with stop and rm when finished.
Dockerfile for static HTML (nginx:alpine)
# Use a lightweight Nginx image as base
FROM nginx:alpine

# Copy our custom index.html into the Nginx web root
COPY index.html /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html

# Expose port 80 (Nginx default)
EXPOSE 80

# Command to run Nginx (default for nginx:alpine image)
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]
This builds an image that, when run, serves your static page. Rebuild the image after editing index.html to update the content.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Troubleshooting Tips
screens.narratorSegment: When working with Docker, several common mistakes can impede progress. First, permission denied errors occur if the user is not in the docker group; this is fixed by adding the user to the group and applying the change with a new group session. Second, services appear unreachable when port mapping is omitted or uses the wrong host port; always confirm the -p host:container mapping and check the host firewall if ports are blocked. Third, attempting to remove a running container without stopping it will fail; follow the stop-then-remove sequence. Fourth, stale stopped containers and unused images accumulate and consume disk space over time; incorporate regular pruning into your maintenance routine. A practical debug flow: verify the daemon with hello-world, confirm your user can run docker, check running containers with docker ps, inspect container logs if a service fails, and then stop and remove containers if you need to redeploy. Example: if your Nginx page does not appear, verify the container is running, check mapped ports, and inspect container logs for startup errors. Takeaway: a short checklist—daemon, permissions, port mapping, logs, cleanup—resolves most early problems.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Troubleshooting Tips
Quick checklist
  • Is the Docker daemon running? Use the hello-world check.
  • Is your user in the docker group to avoid permission errors?
  • Is port mapping correct and not blocked by a firewall?
  • Have you inspected container logs for runtime errors?
  • Are old containers or images consuming disk space?
Example fix flow
If a web page is not reachable: confirm the container is running, verify host-to-container port mapping, inspect docker logs for the container, and ensure the index.html is present inside the image. Rebuild the image if necessary.
Common mistake
Assuming a stopped container still serves content. Stopped containers do not run processes; remove and restart or rebuild if required.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you'll build a practical understanding of containers with Docker and why containers matter for a Linux professional. We'll start by defining containerization and contrast it with virtual machines so you can see why containers are lighter and faster. Then we'll walk through installing the Docker Engine on a Linux host, verifying the installation, and running a simple container to confirm everything works. After that we explore images and containers — how to pull images from a registry and run them with common options like detached mode and port mapping. Finally you will learn how to author a simple Dockerfile, build a custom image, and run your own containerized web page. As you learn, pay attention to common pitfalls such as permission errors when the user is not in the docker group, and the tendency to forget to remove stopped containers which consumes disk space. By the end you will be able to install Docker, run an official image like Nginx, examine running containers, and build a small custom image from a Dockerfile. Think about a service you manage now — could it be packaged and moved between systems more reliably if it ran in a container?

In this set of objectives we focus on practical, verifiable skills you will acquire. First, you'll be able to explain containerization and how it differs from virtual machines. That means you can describe the sharing of a host kernel, why containers start faster, and why they are more resource efficient. Second, you will install the Docker Engine on a Linux host, including adding the official repository, installing the docker-ce package, and configuring your user to run Docker commands without sudo. Third, you'll pull and run images from a public registry, using common run options such as detached mode and port mapping to expose services. Finally, you will manage containers: listing running and stopped containers, stopping and removing containers, and understanding the cleanup steps to reclaim disk space. Each objective pairs a concrete action with why that action matters in a real environment, so you can both perform commands and explain their purpose. As you work through the hands-on lab, verify each milestone by running commands and observing expected output; that practice converts knowledge into a reliable skill set.

This second objectives slide emphasizes operational practices and safety checks you will perform. First, you will learn to verify the Docker daemon is running and that your user can communicate with it; this prevents common permission errors that block progress. Second, you will practice running a pre-built Nginx container and confirming service availability via port mapping so you understand host-to-container networking basics. Third, you'll author a Dockerfile, build an image, and learn how each Dockerfile instruction creates layers; understanding layers helps with small, cache-friendly builds. Fourth, you'll learn cleanup and troubleshooting basics: how to list stopped containers, remove unused images, and recognize when disk space may be consumed by leftover artifacts. Each objective pairs a measurable command or file edit with the explanation of why it matters in production or during testing. Completing these objectives will leave you able to deploy a simple web page using Docker and to explain the operational steps you followed when asked.

Containerization packages an application together with its runtime, libraries, and configuration so that the complete runtime environment moves as a single unit. For a Linux administrator that means fewer environment mismatches: a container carries the app and dependencies but uses the host kernel rather than a full guest operating system. In practice this makes containers much lighter and faster: starting a container takes seconds, while booting a full VM may take minutes. A concrete example is running a web server. With a VM you maintain a full OS image plus Nginx; with a container you package just Nginx and its minimal libraries and start it instantly. A common misconception is to treat containers as tiny virtual machines; this can lead to unnecessary duplication and heavier images. Instead, think of containers as isolated processes with limited scope and predictable file systems. When you design services, prefer each container to run a single concern and use configuration or orchestration for composition. Takeaway: containers improve portability and startup speed by sharing the host kernel, but they are not replacements for a full OS when you need separate kernels or deep hardware abstraction. How would you separate concerns in an application you support today so each part can run in its own container?

Let's contrast containers and virtual machines with concrete trade-offs a Linux engineer needs to know. Containers package applications and dependencies but share the host kernel. That means low overhead, faster startup, and greater density—more containers per host. Virtual machines emulate hardware and include a full guest OS, which increases resource consumption but provides a separate kernel and stronger isolation at the cost of slower provisioning. A practical scenario: running many identical microservices benefits from containers because each instance consumes fewer resources and starts quickly. Conversely, if you must run an alternative kernel version or isolate kernel modules, a VM is the safer choice. A common misconception is that containers automatically provide stronger security isolation than VMs. In reality, the kernel is shared, so policy, namespaces, and cgroups matter; containers should be combined with security controls when isolation is required. Example: on a test host you might run ten container instances of a web app; attempting the same with full VMs likely exhausts memory or C P U far sooner. Takeaway: pick containers for efficiency and portability, pick VMs when you need full OS separation or complete kernel isolation. Ask yourself: which constraints matter more—density and speed, or kernel-level separation?

Installing Docker Engine on a Debian or Ubuntu system includes a few precise steps: prepare packages for secure transport, add Docker's GPG key so the repository is trusted, add Docker's stable repository, and then install docker-ce along with the CLI and container runtime. The commands shown in the lesson content are the recommended sequence. Practically, you will update apt, install supporting packages for HTTPS transport, register Docker's repository key, and then install docker-ce, docker-ce-cli and containerd. io. A crucial operational step is adding your user to the docker group so you can run docker commands without sudo; forgetting this step commonly results in permission denied messages. After installation, verify the daemon is active and test with the hello-world image, which performs a simple run and prints a success message when the runtime is healthy. Misconception: running docker commands as root permanently is not recommended for day-to-day work; instead, use group membership for safety and convenience. Takeaway: follow the install sequence exactly and verify with the hello-world run to ensure the engine operates correctly. Install Docker Engine on Linux means add repository, install docker-ce and dependencies, and add your user to the docker group to avoid permission errors.. In practical terms, repository, package, and group setup for debian/ubuntu. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

After installing Docker you must verify that the daemon is active and that you can run containers. A standard verification is to run the lightweight hello-world image. This image performs a simple runtime check and prints a success message when Docker can fetch and run an image. If the daemon is not running, the hello-world run will fail. Another common issue appears as a permission denied error when the current user is not in the docker group; you can fix this by adding the user to that group and applying the change immediately with a new group session. Concrete example: after installation run the hello-world image and then list running containers. If the hello-world image completes successfully it prints a confirmation message and exits; it may not leave a running container. Misconception: assuming a successful install means you can run long-lived services immediately without checking group membership and daemon status can lead to confusing failures during later steps. Key takeaway: always verify the daemon with hello-world and set correct permissions before moving to real services. Verify Docker: hello-world and permissions means run hello-world to check the daemon and add your user to the docker group to avoid permission denied errors.. In practical terms, confirming the daemon, running the test image, and avoiding permission errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Docker uses two fundamental artifacts: images and containers. An image is a build-time, read-only package that contains everything needed to run an application: code, libraries, system tools, and default settings. Images are built from a Dockerfile and composed of layers where each instruction typically creates a new layer that can be cached. A container is a runnable instance of an image — a process (or set of processes) with its own filesystem and namespaces. For example, you can pull the Ubuntu image from a registry and then instantiate a container from it to run commands inside that environment. This separation matters because you can build many identical containers from a single image; images are the portable artifact you store in registries such as Docker Hub. A common mistake is editing a running container's filesystem and assuming the change is preserved to a new image; instead, you should update the Dockerfile and rebuild so the change is reproducible. Takeaway: treat images as immutable build artifacts and containers as ephemeral runtime instances that you can stop and remove. How would you capture a change in configuration so it survives image rebuilds?

Pulling an image retrieves it from a registry and stores it locally. Use the pull command to download an image before running it, although many run commands will pull an image automatically if it's missing. When you run an image as a container, common options include detached mode and port mapping so services are accessible from the host. For example, running an Nginx container mapping container port eighty to host port eight thousand eighty makes the web server reachable from a browser. Another important option is naming containers so you can refer to them easily when stopping or removing them. A frequent operator misstep is forgetting the port mapping and then wondering why the service is unreachable; always confirm the -p or port mapping semantics. Concrete example: pull the ubuntu image and run a shell, or pull the nginx image and run it detached while mapping ports. Takeaway: use pull to control when you fetch artifacts, and use docker run flags to configure networking and lifecycle behavior for the container instance. Pulling and Running Images means use docker pull to fetch images and docker run with flags like detached mode and port mapping to make services reachable.. A Dockerfile is the recipe Docker uses to build an image. Each instruction creates a layer that contributes to the final image: FROM selects the base image, RUN executes commands during build, COPY brings files from the build context into the image, EXPOSE documents ports the container listens on, and CMD declares the default command that runs when a container starts. When working with Docker, several common mistakes can impede progress. First, permission denied errors occur if the user is not in the docker group; this is fixed by adding the user to the group and applying the change with a new group session. Second, services appear unreachable when port mapping is omitted or uses the wrong host port; always confirm the -p host:container mapping and check the host firewall if ports are blocked. Third, attempting to remove a running container without stopping it will fail; follow the stop-then-remove sequence. Fourth, stale stopped containers and unused images accumulate and consume disk space over time; incorporate regular pruning into your maintenance routine. A practical debug flow: verify the daemon with hello-world, confirm your user can run docker, check running containers with docker ps, inspect container logs if a service fails, and then stop and remove containers if you need to redeploy. Example: if your Nginx page does not appear, verify the container is running, check mapped ports, and inspect container logs for startup errors. Takeaway: a short checklist—daemon, permissions, port mapping, logs, cleanup—resolves most early problems.
